displayQuote: Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them

meta.title: Who really said "Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yeats almost certainly said it — to two English dons at Oxford. But it survives only in a friend’s recollection, printed in 1955.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them'?
meta.ogDescription: W. B. Yeats, overheard at Oxford. The sole record is L. A. G. Strong's 1955 memoir — sixteen years after Yeats died.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1865–1939 · Irish poet, dramatist and mystic; Nobel Prize for Literature, 1923
answer.sourceLine: Yeats said it aloud, not in print. The novelist and critic L. A. G. Strong — a long-time friend of the poet — overheard him say it to two English dons and reported it in “Yeats at His Ease” in The London Magazine for March 1955, on page 57. That single article is the whole documented basis for the line: no manuscript, no letter, no essay of Yeats’s own contains it, and Strong published his recollection sixteen years after Yeats’s death. Quote Investigator ↗ accepts it and says so plainly — while noting that “the long delay detracts from the solidity of the testimony.”
answer.confidenceText: Attributed — spoken, not written, and recorded once, from memory, long afterwards.

source.excerpt: Yeats in my hearing remarked to two English dons, ‘I can’t see what you think you are achieving. You seem to be busy with the propagation of second and third and fourth hand opinions upon literature. Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them.’
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ traces the sentence to one source: L. A. G. Strong’s article “Yeats at His Ease” in The London Magazine: A Monthly Review of Literature, volume 2, number 3, March 1955 — article start page 56, quotation on page 57.

Its conclusion is an acceptance with a caveat attached, and we have kept the caveat: “the words of W. B. Yeats were overheard by Leonard Strong when Yeats was at Oxford, and Strong shared the quotation in an article published many years later in 1955. The long delay detracts from the solidity of the testimony, but the vividness of the opinion may have produced a durable memory in Strong’s mind.”

Every later appearance QI documents traces back through Strong rather than around him — James Johnson Sweeney’s Vision and Image: A Way of Seeing (1968), quotation page 119, and Monk Gibbon’s “The Yeats I Knew” in E. H. Mikhail’s W. B. Yeats: Interviews and Recollections (1977), article start page 372, quotation page 378. There is no independent contemporary witness.

We read Wikiquote’s William Butler Yeats page ↗ in full — a long, heavily sourced page organised work by work. The sentence does not appear anywhere on it, in any section. That absence is the point: this is a remark, not a text.

Dates checked independently: Yeats, 13 June 1865 – 28 January 1939 ↗, and Leonard Alfred George Strong, 8 March 1896 – 17 August 1958 ↗, who published as L. A. G. Strong. Strong was writing three years before his own death, about a friend who had been dead for sixteen.
source.cutTag: L. A. G. Strong, “Yeats at His Ease”, 1955
source.excerptNote: That is the passage as Quote Investigator reproduces it ↗ from page 57. The famous sentence is the last of three, and the two before it are what give it its edge: Yeats is not talking about culture in the abstract, he is telling two academics to their faces what he thinks of their trade. We could not consult the 1955 issue of The London Magazine ourselves; the wording and the page locator are QI’s.

source.rightsNote: Most of Yeats’s own work published before 1931 is in the public domain in the United States — but this sentence is not from it. The only text that carries the wording is Strong’s article of March 1955, which is well inside copyright. Quoting the sentence itself is ordinary attributed quotation; reproducing Strong’s passage at length is not.

author.heading: About W. B. Yeats
author.metaLine: 1865–1939 · Irish poet, dramatist and mystic · Nobel Prize for Literature, 1923
author.bio: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was an Irish symbolist poet, dramatist and mystic, awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1923 and later the compiler of the Oxford Book of Modern Verse. He came to live at Oxford in 1919, in what his friend L. A. G. Strong remembered as a productive and happy period. He was a formidable talker as well as a writer, which is why a number of the lines people quote from him — this one included — were spoken rather than published.

copyAttribution: "Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them." — W. B. Yeats, overheard at Oxford and recorded by L. A. G. Strong in "Yeats at His Ease," The London Magazine, March 1955, page 57. Yeats never wrote it down; the line survives only in Strong's recollection, published sixteen years after Yeats's death.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Yeats came to live at Oxford in 1919, and Strong records him there as productive and happy — and, on this occasion, sharp. The remark lands on two dons in the business of literary opinion, and its claim is deliberately backwards: that being cultured means holding fewer views, not more.

It has since become a favourite of people arguing against received opinion, usually stripped of the scene that produced it. Restored to that scene it is less a maxim than a put-down, delivered to the faces of the men it was about.
context.pull: Not a maxim about culture. A put-down, delivered to two dons who were listening.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI traces the quotation to L. A. G. Strong, 'Yeats at His Ease', The London Magazine: A Monthly Review of Literature, volume 2, number 3, March 1955, start page 56, quote page 57.

QI reproduces the passage: "Yeats in my hearing remarked to two English dons, 'I can't see what you think you are achieving. You seem to be busy with the propagation of second and third and fourth hand opinions upon literature. Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions, but in getting rid of them.'"

QI's conclusion: 'the words of W. B. Yeats were overheard by Leonard Strong when Yeats was at Oxford, and Strong shared the quotation in an article published many years later in 1955. The long delay detracts from the solidity of the testimony, but the vividness of the opinion may have produced a durable memory in Strong's mind.'
QI states 'Yeats came to live at Oxford in 1919, and Strong says that he was productive and happy there', and describes Strong as a long-time friend of the poet.

QI's later citations are James Johnson Sweeney, Vision and Image: A Way of Seeing (1968), quote page 119; and Monk Gibbon, 'The Yeats I Knew', in E. H. Mikhail (ed.), W. B. Yeats: Interviews and Recollections (1977), start page 372, quote page 378.
Wikiquote's William Butler Yeats page gives his dates as 13 June 1865 to 28 January 1939 and the 1923 Nobel Prize, and contains no instance of this sentence in any section.
Leonard Alfred George Strong (8 March 1896 - 17 August 1958) was an English novelist, critic, historian and poet who published as L. A. G. Strong.
